title: Fight over fossil fuels leaves COP31 climate talks in deadlock
summary: Countries from nearly 200 countries are in a deadlock to try and get a new global climate agreement.
text:
Fight over fossil fuels leaves COP31 climate talks in deadlock
- Published
Negotiations at the COP31 UN climate summit in Turkey are in deadlock, having run more than 24 hours into overtime as countries remain unable to agree on a new global climate deal.
In a late intervention on Friday, a group of countries led by France and Panama pushed back against the draft agreement which included no reference to reducing the world's demand for fossil fuels.
This still remains the main sticking point, along with a push from the Africa Group to get commitments on more money for adaptation - but the EU has previously said it would not support this.
Negotiating teams due to fly out on Sunday morning are now moving their flights to Monday in a sign that a deal is not in sight.
Not all countries have the funding or capacity to do this, and at some point the meeting could lose the critical number of nations needed to pass any global agreement.
This means the summit would end with no deal and have to be suspended. This has only happened once before in the 24 years countries have been meeting.
- More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged 
  - Published1 day ago
Ministers from island states, Panama, and a strong contingent of EU nations which include Spain, France, Belgium, Sweden and Finland have said they are pushing to get a commitment to move away from oil, gas and coal back into the final agreement after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi pushed for its removal.
"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.
His words were echoed by France's Minister of Ecological Transition Monique Barbut.
She took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture, use and storage - the technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground - as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.
"We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," Barbut said.
For the first time at a COP the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - acknowledges that the goal of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed.
The world is entering a period called "overshoot".
Beyond this point scientists warn, external that millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat.
The BBC understands that a number of other EU nations were asked to join the rebellion but declined, considering it unhelpful to negotiations.
Although one lead negotiator said he sympathised: "How can you have a climate agreement with no mention of the cause."
But Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister who is leading negotiations, pushed back.
He argued that this summit was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sourc

title: Killer robots: U.N. talks fall short of hopes for legally binding rules
summary: U.N. talks in Geneva have failed to deliver binding rules on autonomous weapons, as humanitarian groups warn that military AI is advancing far faster than diplomacy.
text:
Killer robots: U.N. talks fall short of hopes for legally binding rules
GENEVA — Diplomats meeting at the United Nations in Geneva have agreed to start discussing options to regulate lethal autonomous weapons, often called "killer robots."
After a week of negotiations that dragged on until the small hours of Saturday morning, a compromise emerged: countries would have two years to suggest regulations that could be legally binding, but could also be optional.
Bleary-eyed negotiators insisted the agreement was better than nothing and showed the U.N.'s disarmament process could still function. But for many humanitarian organizations and many countries, the deal falls far short of what they had hoped for.
Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo.
Their concerns stem from the kind of warfare we are now seeing. In Ukraine, Sudan and Gaza, civilians are being killed by semi-autonomous drones. This year in Sudan, 80% of civilian deaths were caused by drones according to the U.N.
Humans remain, albeit very remotely, in control for now, but humanitarian organizations fear we are on the verge of seeing artificial intelligence-assisted weapons make the decision to kill entirely on their own.
Algorithms making life-and-death decisions
"There is a fundamental ethical concern with having what are essentially these life-and-death decisions determined by programming, determined by an algorithm," said ICRC legal adviser Georgia Hinds. "That's not something that you can fix with better technology. That is a moral red line that we cannot cross."
No one went into the negotiations thinking they would be easy; some of the world's most powerful countries, among them the U.S., Russia and Israel, had already indicated their reluctance to agree to binding regulations.
On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting's agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.
"They're just kicking the can down the road," said one frustrated delegate. As the clock ticked on and the weekend approached, diplomats scrambled to get some kind of result from negotiations that had been billed as a last chance to regulate weapons whose technology and decision-making capabilities we may not even fully understand.
Finally, at 4:30 a.m. on Saturday morning, they emerged from the negotiating room to announce their compromise: no to a deal within a year, maybe to legally binding rules, or maybe not.
A "nothing burger"
The ICRC immediately said it regretted the move and renewed its appeal for a binding treaty. Other campaigners were less polite, calling the deal "a real disappointment" and a "nothing burger." "I am concerned people will die because of this," added another.

title: Judge approves $7.25bn settlement for Roundup weedkiller cancer claims
summary: The settlement will be paid by Bayer to users who already have non-Hodgkin lymphoma and those who fall ill in the future.
text:
Judge approves $7.25bn settlement for Roundup weedkiller cancer claims
- Published
A Missouri judge on Friday approved a $7.25bn (£5.5bn) settlement stemming from lawsuits alleging that Bayer's weedkiller Roundup causes cancer.
Judge Timothy Boyer said the settlement was "fair, reasonable, and adequate".
Bayer, the German bio-tech giant, had proposed paying the $7.25bn to definitively resolve a legal battle in the US.
The nationwide settlement will be paid to Roundup users who are already sick with non-Hodgkin lymphoma and those who fall ill in the future.
The company had already paid roughly $10bn to resolve litigation related to Roundup.
The settlements to participants range from $10,000 to $165,000, depending on how frequently they used the product, when they were diagnosed with the cancer and how severe their illness was.
"[Friday's] final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice," said Christopher Seeger, a court-appointed counsel for cancer patients in the case.
Bayer will make annual payments into a fund for up to 21 years, providing as much as $7.25bn.
Some attorneys had objected to the settlement funds, arguing they were not enough, but the judge said he did not want to delay payouts to sick victims.
Bayer denies that its Roundup product causes cancer.
The settlement comes after the Supreme Court in June ruled in favour of Bayer, overturning a $1.25m settlement for a Missouri man who said Roundup and its ingredient glyphosate was to blame for his non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
The court ruled 7-2, saying Bayer cannot be sued in state courts because federal regulations do not mandate a cancer warning label.
The company has faced thousands of claims in US state and federal courts from people alleging they developed cancer after using the product.
Roundup was developed by Monsanto in the 1970s. Its active ingredient, glyphosate, was identified by the International Agency for Research on Cancer, a unit of the World Health Organization in 2015 as a probable human carcinogen.
Bayer and some other regulators, including the US Environmental Protection Agency, have disputed those findings.
But the issue has forced the company through years of costly litigation in the US, as juries in several states opt to award billions of dollars to users of the herbicide.

title: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
summary: Ukraine's president says Kyiv acted after 109 separate Russian aerial attacks on bridges in Ukraine.
text:
Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
- Published
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.
In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".
He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsular it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.
"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.
The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.
"If Putin used the internet, he could see that."
The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.
This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.
Russian attacks on Ukraine continued on Friday evening and overnight: a seven-year-old boy was killed in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region. Local officials say he had been in a playground at the time.
A 20-year-old female medic was also killed. A local official added that when rescuers rushed to the scene, the same site was targeted again with jet powered drones. Another 58 people were injured in the city.
Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.
"The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said.
He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".
The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence".
Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".
Streeting's description of Putin chimed with the comments made earlier by Zelensky, who described the Kremlin leader a "killer". This was done in response to US President Donald Trump referring this week to Putin as his "friend".

title: Federal jury convicts man of starting the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles
summary: Prosecutors argued the defendant, 30-year-old Jonathan Rinderknecht, had been "mad at everything" in the days leading up to the January 2025 fire, which killed 12 people.
text:
Federal jury convicts man of starting the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles
LOS ANGELES — The man accused of sparking last year's deadly Palisades Fire was found guilty of arson charges Friday after his first federal case earlier this year ended in a mistrial.
Jurors convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of lighting a fire on Jan. 1, 2025, that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up Jan. 7, becoming one of the most destructive wildfires in California history. The Palisades Fire killed 12 people as it incinerated entire neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu.
Rinderknecht pleaded not guilty to federal charges of destruction of property by means of fire and arson. The scope of the first charge was narrowed to only include the Jan. 1 blaze, known as the Lachman Fire, and the second addresses the Palisades Fire. He was convicted on both charges.
With little apparent reaction, Rinderknecht gave his attorneys hugs before leaving the courtroom. The verdict was delivered on the third day of deliberation.
Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in LA, said the verdict was a "testament of the hard work" his team put into the case. He said he was "intimately familiar" with the strength of the evidence and was happy with the jury that convicted Rinderknecht.
Rinderknecht's attorney Steve Haney said in a statement they were disappointed in the verdict but respected the jury process.
"After a lengthy deliberation, they clearly gave this case a great deal of consideration," Haney said. Regarding an appeal, he said they would review all the options at the right time.
Rinderknecht is set to be sentenced March 17, 2027. Each count carries a mandatory minimum of five years and a maximum of 20 years in federal prison.
Prosecutors continued to pursue the case after Rinderknecht's first jury deadlocked 10 to 2 in favor of acquittal after a two-week trial in June. They dropped a third charge of timber set afire when they filed a new indictment for the retrial. Essayli said he believed the first jury acted improperly and appeared to consider things in their decision that weren't presented as evidence during the trial.
Juror says Rinderknecht's own testimony pointed to a guilty verdict
Juror No. 3, who only wanted to be identified by his first name Cameron, said he was the only person who felt Rinderknecht was not guilty at the start of deliberations. Another person was undecided, and the rest of the 10 jurors believed Rinderknecht was guilty.
"It took a lot for me to be convinced otherwise," he said. "After listening to every single point, I do now agree that he's guilty."
Cameron said he initially had concerns about a technical review conducted by a defense expert witness, who argued the government had gotten the origin area of the fire wrong. He said there was a "lack of information" presented to the jury about the technical review.

title: Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out
summary: Fausto Isidro "Chapo Idisro" Meza Flores, who is accused of drug trafficking and torture, is detained after gun fight with authorities.
text:
Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out
- Published
A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.
Fausto Isidro "Chapo Idisro" Meza Flores was detained along with his lieutenant by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition.
Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House.
Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile.
Using US intelligence on his whereabouts, Mexican special forces descended on his location using "stealth and surprise", establishing a perimeter to prevent him from escaping and reinforcements arriving, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
However, they "came under attack from gunfire and explosives" before entering the property and arresting Meza Flores and his second-in-command, it added.
Videos circulating online appear to show helicopters firing streams of bullets towards the ground in Guasave. Others appear to show people at a baseball stadium fleeing as they hear shooting sounds.
The two detainees were subsequently flown to Mexico City to face prosecution, the defence secretariat said.
When he was added to the FBI's most-wanted list in 2025, he was accused of "heinous crimes" including kidnapping, extortion and torture.
Then-acting FBI director Brian Driscoll said Meza Flores and his organisation had also unleashed a "scourge of illicit drugs" into the US via its southern border with Mexico.
He was initially charged with drug trafficking in the US in 2012 before being charged again in 2019.
The 44-year-old is alleged to have conspired to manufacture and distribute large quantities of cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana between 2005 and 2019.
Meza Flores was originally a high-ranking member of the Beltrán Leyva Organization, but a split between rival factions led to a surge of violence and prompted him to establish his own cartel by 2013.
His organisation has also engaged in what US officials described as an "extremely violent turf war" with the Sinaloa Cartel, one of the most powerful drug trafficking gangs, which operates in the same region.
Meza Flores was added to the FBI's most-wanted list after Mexican authorities reportedly linked his cartel to 20 million fentanyl pills they seized in 2024.

title: Deal with EU not dependent on tuition fees agreement, Miliband says
summary: Brussels sources had previously suggested the bloc might not apply the wider deal until fees were lowered for EU students in Britain.
text:
Deal with EU not dependent on tuition fees agreement, Miliband says
- Published
A deal agreed between the UK and the European Union on Friday will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can negotiate a separate tuition fees agreement, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has told the BBC.
The measures agreed in Brussels include scrapping most checks on British food exports in return for the UK following some EU regulations from 2028, and a new youth mobility scheme.
However, a proposal from the bloc to lower the level of tuition fees paid by EU students in the UK has not been agreed.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was "confident" a solution would be found, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham adding "me too" during a press conference announcing the deal.
Meanwhile, asked in his interview with the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether rejoining the EU would be looked at, Miliband said "all the options will be on the table".
It came after the prime minister said that he would discuss possible ideas for even closer ties with the bloc in the coming months.
- What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start? 
  - Published23 hours ago
- Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more 
  - Published23 hours ago
- Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow 
  - Published22 hours ago
UK and EU leaders have hailed the closer cooperation agreement, with Burnham calling the deal a "win-win" that could lower the cost of living and reduce red tape.
The prime minister said the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year.
EU sources had earlier suggested that the bloc might hold up applying the wider deal until it was agreed that EU students who wanted to study in the UK would pay the same fees as British students.
Miliband said it was "absolutely clear" the agreements on food exports, energy and youth mobility would apply, even though there has not been a deal on tuition fees.
"President von der Leyen... was very clear about this at the press conference we just had. She said there are those three agreements and then there's a separate piece of paper and a separate issue, which is looking at the issue of tuition," he said.
Asked again whether the agreements would definitely become law, the foreign secretary said: "Yes, absolutely."
"The dates are set out in 2028 when these things are coming in, we're introducing legislation in Parliament, so definitely."
Miliband said there would be "no cost" to the UK taxpayer for anything agreed at Friday's summit, adding that there would be no new contributions to the EU budget.
He said previously announced agreements on EU schemes like Erasmus+ were a "separate decision" and the summit "was not about cost to the taxpayer".
Speaking on Friday, Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".

title: Perspective: Defining 'human'
summary: The Cambridge Dictionary has chosen the word "human" as its Word of the Year. Why ever might a word that entered the English language over 500 years ago be so honored?
text:
Perspective: Defining 'human'
The Cambridge Dictionary has revealed its Word of the Year for 2026. It won't need much explanation. Unlike "parasocial," their 2025 word, which refers to an unreciprocated emotional connection, perhaps with a chatbot, or 2018's word, "nomophobia," which is an irrational fear of having no mobile phone service–although, given all the recent cyber-struggles, why would that be irrational?
The Cambridge 2026 World of the Year is … human. As in us. And perhaps humanity could stand some recognition in times when people see Artificial Intelligence seep into our lives the way ancient dinosaurs may have watched the asteroid plunge through the atmosphere, and think, "They're coming for us!" though I suspect a few T-Rexes might have said, "Hey, don't worry! We're too big to fail!"
Cambridge defines "human" as: "(h)aving the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines," but they don't specify much about what those qualities, faults and feelings are.
I'd say that humans have a sense of responsibility. We can say, "I'm sorry, that's my fault," when we screw up or fall short, as opposed to screens that just flash, SYSTEM OVERLOAD or UPDATE IN PROGRESS, 12% COMPLETE.
Humans seek joy, not just continued existence. Laughter, tears, love, spice, poetry, and all that jazz, not just code or text. Humans like jokes and prayers. We're driven by feelings, not just steered by algorithms. Love, fear, anger, desire, joy, and courage, excited by events, nerves and hormones – combine to make us unpredictable, irreverent and unreliable. But our experiences can also instill judgement; an appreciation for what's important; what endures; and what makes the lives we have worth living and savoring.
Making human the 2026 Word of the Year may remind us that we human beings, unlike any robots we have yet devised, have a sense of our own fragility. We know we don't last forever. And so it is important to strive, laugh, and love while we have the chance. The Cambridge dictionary leaves what human truly means to us.

title: Ghanaian boy killed in US 'deserved so much better', says New York Mayor Mamdani
summary: At the funeral for the 15-year-old who was fatally shot last month, Mamdani spoke alongside the boy's father and civil rights leaders.
text:
Ghanaian boy killed in US 'deserved so much better', says New York Mayor Mamdani
- Published
A 15-year-old Ghanaian boy who was killed in the US last month was remembered as a hard-working student with dreams of becoming a doctor, as his father, New York City's mayor and civil rights leaders gave eulogies during his funeral on Friday.
Javits Frimpong was shot and killed while walking to school in the Bronx. His death has sparked outrage in both Ghana and the US, and reignited debates about gun violence in America.
"Javits deserved so much better and so do every single one of you," Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. "Though he was only a New Yorker for a short time, New York City will forever be proud to call Javits one of our own."
Frimpong moved to the US about a year before the shooting.
"I worked hard to bring you from Ghana to America because I wanted you to have opportunities, a better future, and a chance to achieve everything that you dreamed of," his father, Thomas Frimpong, said.
His mother was granted an emergency visa from Ghana to mourn her son at Friday's funeral service, following Mamdani's lobbying of President Donald Trump earlier this month.
Earlier this month, she told the BBC that she wanted "justice for my son", a sentiment echoed at Friday's service.
Officials have said they are exploring several motives. Frimpong's family has said he experienced bullying at school, which police said they were investigating.
Frimpong was chased down and shot on 29 October. He was taken to a local hospital, where he was pronounced dead.
Police have said three teenage boys were involved in the shooting. A 17-year-old has been arrested and charged with murder, and will be tried as an adult. Police are still searching for the other two.
"Gun violence is never the answer," Ben Crump, an attorney representing the family, said at the funeral as he vowed to seek justice for Frimpong.
Ghana's government has condemned the killing and said it would follow the case closely to ensure justice was achieved.
It has urged US authorities to conduct a thorough investigation and said it was ready to provide legal and consular support to ensure the perpetrators were brought to justice.

title: FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database
summary: The National Crime Information Center database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information.
text:
FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database
- Published
The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal information database, US media reports, citing two people briefed on the issue.
The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks. The BBC contacted the FBI for comment.
This comes after a string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors in the US last week. Officials have said they were not caused by cyberattacks, but the blackouts have sparked scrutiny from lawmakers.
White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired this week, with US President Donald Trump saying he was not good enough.
It would not be the first time hackers have targeted the FBI, the domestic intelligence and security service of the US.
In September, the FBI said it was investigating an apparent breach by a cyber-crime group ShinyHunters, which claimed it had stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff - around 38,000 people.
After that hack, one former FBI agent told the BBC he feared for the safety of current employees, whose personal information could soon become available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.
In a separate development, NBC reported an apparent cyberattack against the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) .
Employees were informed on Thursday that its farm payment system had been targeted, NBC said.
The USDA has not publicly commented on the issue.

title: They were fined $811m for conning detained migrants, but the scams didn't stop
summary: How convicted fraudsters made millions from detained immigrants, evaded efforts to shut down their bail business and left migrants behind bars.
text:
They were fined $811m for conning detained migrants, but the scams didn't stop
- Published
Every morning for a month, Mildred Juarez woke up at five to be the first person in the showers at the immigration centre in Texas where she was being detained. Her friends had paid her bail, and she wanted to look presentable when she was finally released.
But every day, she was told her bond had not been paid.
Juarez was confused. Her friends had wired $2,600 (£1,970) to a bond company, Libre Immigration Services (LIS), that had been recommended by her lawyer. LIS said it would begin "the process of paying her immigration bond". But the next day came, and the day after that, with no release.
What she didn't know was that LIS was owned by a convicted fraudster, who had acquired the assets of another bail company co-founded by two men who also had fraud convictions. These two men were fined $811m in 2024 for scamming their clients.
Their firm, Libre By Nexus, which was at one point the largest immigration bail company in America, had appeared to shut down after federal regulators caught up with them.
But public records and BBC interviews with clients and former employees reveal a tangle of interconnected operations continued - along with the flow of cash - while leaving immigrants stuck in detention centres.
Since President Donald Trump has returned to office after promising an immigration crackdown, Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has made over 1.2m arrests, and fast-tracked deportations. The administration has tried unsuccessfully to make it illegal to give migrants bail but the sharp increase in detentions has increased demand for bond companies to secure bail and their release.
Conditions in these centres can be poor. Held in custody, away from family, often scared to speak out, many have faced health problems and endured inadequate food or treatment, according to immigrant advocates and reports by the US government.
In the detention centre where Juarez was locked up, she and about 100 other detainees slept in bunks laid out in rows in a cacophonous room. The lights were left on all night and guards routinely woke everyone up for roll call. According to Castro and advocacy groups, detainees who caused trouble were put in "the hold" - solitary confinement.
The White House and officials from Homeland Security did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.
For Juarez, the wait to be bailed out of detention seemed interminable.
In an email to the BBC, a spokesperson for LIS said Juarez "misunderstands" their services - that they are not bondsmen themselves, but they connect detained individuals to those who are licensed bondsmen. They said another company ultimately decided not to work with her.
An email sent by LIS, and reviewed by the BBC, said that the company had paid a cash bond to ICE on behalf of Juarez. The message was forwarded to Juarez as proof of payment a few days before her release.

title: Trafalgar Square Christmas tree felled in Norway
summary: The 21m tree is Oslo’s annual thank you for Britain’s support during World War Two.
text:
Trafalgar Square Christmas tree felled in Norway
- Published
This year's Trafalgar Square Christmas tree has been cut down in a forest outside Oslo, ready to begin its journey to London.
The 21m (69ft) tree, nicknamed Jolly Cheery, is about 75 years old. It was felled on Friday by the Lord Mayor of Westminster, Karen Scarborough, and the Mayor of Oslo, Anne Lindboe.
Norway has sent a tree to the capital every year since 1947 as a thank you for Britain's support during World War Two, when King Haakon VII and the Norwegian government lived in exile in London.
Its lights will be switched on by the two mayors at a ceremony in the square on Thursday, 3 December.
Scarborough said: "It's my greatest honour to take part in this wonderful tradition for both the cities of Oslo and London.
"This tree is a powerful symbol of friendship and peace, reminding us to be there for one another during the festive period."
Scarborough thanked "the people of Oslo and Norway for this truly fabulous gift" and added: "With the care and dedication of the team, I'm sure it will look magnificent on Trafalgar Square."
Lindboe said: "Oslo has been sending a Christmas tree to London for almost eight decades, and every year we send a tree across the North Sea with the same message: we have not forgotten.
"The tradition has a powerful history, and its message remains just as relevant today.
"I hope Jolly Cheery spreads warmth and Christmas cheer to everyone who passes by, and reminds us how much it means to be there for one another, especially in difficult times."
For the second year running, the tree was chosen with the help of a social media poll.
Organisers said it would travel by road in Norway and England using only electric and biodiesel vehicles, cutting the journey's carbon footprint by 80%. It will cross the North Sea on a regular cargo ship from the port of Brevik.
Once in London, it will be decorated in the traditional Norwegian style, with 25m strings of festoon lighting fitted with energy-efficient bulbs.

A mathematician who works for artificial intelligence giant Anthropic claims he has solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of the company's AI tool Claude.
It marks the second time in recent months that an AI company or someone linked to one claims to have cracked a famed unsolved math problem.
Levent Alpöge, a member of the company's technical staff, made the announcement Friday by way of a four-page explanation posted on his website. He said that he believes by working with Claude, he has found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.
"Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," Alpöge wrote. "No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line."
Formulated in 1859, the Riemann Hypothesis centers on the distribution of prime numbers — those that are only divisible by one and themselves — as they grow towards infinity.
Alpöge said his discovery came late Sunday night. He messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to ask about "my ability to announce," as the San Francisco-based company was about to make major news with its stock market debut.
A day after the company's initial public offering — the most valuable in history — Alpöge revealed he'd solved the problem that has proved elusive for more than 150 years. Anthropic did not respond to an email from The Associated Press requesting comment on Alpöge's claim.
Alpöge released his and Claude's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis within 17 million lines of Lean code, a programing language that allows people to program proofs of mathematical theorems. Traditionally the findings buried in that code would be published in a formal paper, said Alex Kontorovich, distinguished professor and department chair of mathematics at Rutgers University.
"Usually when somebody gives you a paper, that's also kind of code for a proof and you have to actually read the paper, follow it yourself, figure out if you believe every single line in that paper. And when you're done, you should have a deep understanding of why something is true," he said.
He said Claude followed that code and said the proof is true.
"Does that mean I understand it? Not yet. But the computer is extraordinarily picky, way pickier than I am and so if you can satisfy the computer, there's a very, very good chance you're going to satisfy me too," he said. "But I have to do the work."
Hours after the announcement, the Riemann Hypothesis remained listed as unsolved on the Clay Mathematics Institute's website. The institute had selected the hypothesis back in 2000 as one of seven Millennium Prize Problems and offered a reward of $1 million for the solution.
The assessment process of whether the problem has actually been solved takes time, explained Martin Bridson, president of the institute.

title: Trump says US flight systems are 'ancient' but 'safe' after ground stop
summary: Trump backed members of his administration who are asking for $50bn to rebuild air traffic control systems in the wake of last Friday's major outage.
text:
Trump says US flight systems are 'ancient' but 'safe' after ground stop
- Published
US President Donald Trump has said air traffic control systems that manage flights across the country are "ancient" and is pushing Congress to fund costly upgrades.
Trump called the systems "obsolete", saying they were at least "55 years old" and noted some towers were not in good shape structurally.
"It's very safe. But it's safe for a different reason because we do it very slowly," he said. "In other words, we travel slower. That's why you have lots of waits at the airport."
His remarks came a week after a historic ground stop halted flights across the US for hours - the longest such event since the terror attacks on 11 September 2001.
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) officials said the agency planned on Friday to share more information about what led to the four-hour ground stop on 13 November.
Top aviation officials within the Trump administration have previously said the cause was related to old equipment overloading, as well as updates to systems.
At a press briefing, Trump responded to some concerns about whether the ground stop issue was at all linked to other tech outages in the same week.
"They're all separate events," he said. "You know we have thousands of companies that are upgrading right now, and when they upgrade, bad things happen."
US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has explained a government contractor was upgrading an aviation telecommunications network, swapping out copper lines for fibre and installing a router, which directs traffic across the network.
The switch led the router to start flooding others in the air traffic control system, sending 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. It is unclear whether the root cause of the issue was the wire replacement or a fault with the router.
As a result, 17 out of 22 air route traffic control centres in the US experienced issues with voice and ground communications. It took the aviation authority 45 minutes to identify where the problem was because maintenance is logged manually on paper.
More than 15,000 flights in the US were delayed or cancelled the day of the outage, according to data from flight tracking sites, affecting an estimated 1.5mn passengers.
Ripple effects from the incident caused issues for days, with thousands more flights being cancelled or delayed over the weekend.
In some cases, passengers were left stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or return to gates.
The ground stop also had a knock-on effect on schedules around the world, with some flights out of the UK and Europe cancelled.

title: Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend
summary: Earlier this week, Trump greeted Putin ahead of a meeting in China and said the pair have a "great relationship".
text:
Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend
- Published
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Vladimir Putin is a "killer" in response to Donald Trump referring to the Russian leader as his "friend" in China this week.
Speaking to CNN, Zelensky said it was up to the US president "how to call Putin" but "for us, he is an enemy... for us, he's a killer".
Before Thursday's historic trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Putin, Trump called Putin his "friend" and said the two leaders have had a "great relationship for many years".
Russian attacks continued overnight, with two people killed, including a boy, and 52 injured in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region, officials said.
Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.
On Friday, at least nine people were killed in Russian strikes targeting bridges in the capital Kyiv and railway stations in western Ukraine - with Zelensky calling the attack the "biggest this year" after an onslaught of 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic, and more than 400 drones.
The strikes came days after Ukraine had badly damaged the Crimean Bridge.
Hours after Friday's strikes on Ukraine, Trump told reporters at the White House that Putin would "love to end the war".
"They [Zelensky and Putin] both want to end it and it's a very good thing I have a relationship," he said on Friday.
Trump also doubled down on his description of the Russian leader as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether Putin is a friend to the US.
However Zelensky said despite Trump's stance, he saw Putin as "a killer".
"I think mostly for the people in the world, he is a killer because he's killing - by the way- he's killing each day and night," he told CNN.
Zelensky also said speaking about Putin like he was a "friend" meant "he doesn't feel enough pressure".
The war of words came as neighbouring Poland said a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace in the south-east of the country early on Friday.
Polish Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said the missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
This was about 100km from where European troops - from 11 of the 36 member nations of the coalition of the willing - were completing a training exercise, Polish authorities said. Another cruise missile and a jet-powered drone were suspected to have hit two other locations, they added.
On Saturday, Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski told the BBC the cruise missiles had guidance systems, so "it is very unlikely that they veered off course as a result of Ukrainian electronic warfare".
"This is a war in Europe that affects our security," he told Radio 4's Today programme, also referencing similar incidents in recent months across Europe.

title: 5 ways to turn off your 'work brain' after the day ends
summary: Don't let your work troubles follow you home. Psychologist Guy Winch shares techniques to help you stop ruminating about your nine-to-five, so you can focus on what really matters.
text:
5 ways to turn off your 'work brain' after the day ends
Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox.
If you're spending your free time spinning your wheels about something that happened at work, guess what? You're still on the clock, says psychologist Guy Winch.
" Your workday only ends when you stop thinking about work," he says.
Winch, author of Mind Over Grind: How to Break Free When Work Hijacks Your Life, says it doesn't have to be this way. In his book, published this year, he shares strategies on how to reclaim your time, energy and attention if work takes up too much of your mental bandwidth.
"Very few of us sit through the evening reliving the glory of the joke that landed in the meeting," he says. "What we do spend hours on are when we get interrupted, dismissed, about the project we're behind on."
That kind of ruminative thinking can have negative effects on our health. Research has shown that it activates our stress response, contributes to poor sleep and eating and, over time, can increase our risks for cardiovascular disease and depression.
Winch, co-host of the podcast Dear Therapists, shares quick strategies you can try if work is taking over your life.
The problem: You can't stop thinking about work
The fix: Take 15 minutes to come up with a solution
Let's say you're trying to focus on your kid's volleyball game but all you can think about is how your colleague keeps taking credit for your work.
Instead of reliving the issue, which is unproductive, take 15 minutes to convert the situation into a problem you can solve, Winch says. "What's the best way of handling it? Do I have a conversation with them? And if I want to have a conversation, what's the outcome I'm trying to get to?"
This approach allows you to create a plan for how to address the situation. "You should feel an ease in stress. Now it will be much easier for you to let go," he says.
The problem: You still can't stop thinking about work
The fix: Distract yourself with a game or a memory task
If you can't stop spinning your wheels about work, try distracting yourself for two or three minutes, Winch says. It can help you reset so you can focus on something else.
"You need something that takes up your mental bandwidth so there's not enough left over for rumination," he says.
He shares a few ideas: Play a puzzle or game like Wordle. Name all the state capitals. Think of whom you sat next to in elementary school. Picture all the items on the top shelf of your fridge.
When you're done, instruct yourself to reengage in whatever you're doing, he says. You might tell yourself, "I really want to enjoy this show now," or "I really want to watch my kid [so I can] talk to her after the game."

The fix: Create boundaries between work and home with immersive rituals

title: Mamdani announces plan to close New York's Rikers Island jail by 2032
summary: Plans to shutter the troubled facility date back to 2019, when the city council first voted to close it but delays arose over where to place inmates.
text:
Mamdani announces plan to close New York's Rikers Island jail by 2032
- Published
New York City's official overseeing the closure of the city's most notorious jail hopes a new plan from Mayor Zohran Mamdani will lead to "a moment of transformation" for how people are detained in the largest US city.
Mamdani on Friday unveiled a plan to close the Rikers Island complex by 2032, to build four new jails and drastically reduce the city's detainee population.
Plans to shutter the troubled facility date back to 2019, when the city council first voted to close it by this year. But plans have been delayed over the years in part due to the logistical difficulties over where to place inmates.
Dana Kaplan - who Mamdani appointed as the city's "Close Rikers Czar" told the BBC News channel on Friday that his latest proposal is not just about getting rid of a decrepit facility.
It is also a "generational opportunity" to "build a different type of detention system" and figure out how to detain people more appropriately, she said.
The Rikers Island jail complex is perched on a 413 acre (167 hectare) island between Queens and the Bronx, and has earned a variety of nicknames over the years because of its dilapidated conditions, including Gladiator School and Torture Island. The jail has housed a number of high-profile inmates awaiting trial, including Tupac Shakur, DMX and Harvey Weinstein.
It houses more than 6,500 inmates at a given time. Mamdani hopes to reduce that number to 4,100 - a goal that has been met with skepticism by the New York City correction officers' union.
"[B]uilding a new system that puts an arbitrary cap on the City's available jail beds is ill-conceived, irresponsible and jeopardizes the safety of all New Yorkers, including our Officers," NYC Correction Officers' Benevolent Association said in a statement. "The City cannot keep the jail population at around 4,100 without irresponsibly releasing individuals who committed violent felony charges."
Kaplan disagreed.
"It's actually possible to have fewer people in jail in New York City - and that is what we should be planning for," she said.
The jail complex has long faced backlash over staffing shortages, crumbling conditions and inmate deaths in the facility, including nine this year. Legislation required the jail to be shuttered by 2027, but Mamdani blamed lags under former Mayor Eric Adams' administration as well as the Covid pandemic for the delays.
Last year, under Adams, a federal judge removed Rikers from the city's control, appointing an independent outside official to make decisions concerning the facility.
In an 88-page report released on Friday, Mamdani said Rikers was a product of "deteriorating infrastructure" and that officials had a "moral imperative" to close it.
New York City Council must approve the updated timeline, with members, including the city's speaker, indicating they support the plan.

title: Man convicted of starting Palisades fire in Los Angeles
summary: The 30-year-old LA resident was convicted of arson leading to wildfires that killed 12 people and destroyed more than 6,800 buildings.
text:
Man convicted of starting Palisades fire in Los Angeles
- Published
A jury in Los Angeles has found a 30-year-old man guilty of starting one of the most destructive wildfires in California's history.
Jonathan Rinderknecht was convicted of arson after starting the fires that swept through Pacific Palisades and parts of Malibu in January last year, killing 12 people and destroying more than 6,800 buildings in the US state.
The conviction was handed down nearly five months after deadlocked jurors led to the judge declaring a mistrial.
Rinderknecht, who had pleaded not guilty, was convicted of two federal charges. He is due to be sentenced on 17 March when he faces between five and 20 years in prison on each charge.
Rinderknecht was found guilty of lighting a fire on 1 January last year which burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up six days later.
One of the charges was for starting the original brush fire, while the other centred on the damage caused when it reignited into a catastrophic blaze.
"We were determined to hold him accountable, and today's guilty verdict delivers a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended," said Bill Essayli, who leads the US Attorney's Office for the Central District of California.
Rinderknecht is a Los Angeles resident and former ride-share delivery driver.
Defence attorney Steve Haney had argued at trial that prosecutors lacked sufficient physical evidence or records to prove their case.
Lawyers for the defendant said they were "disappointed" by the verdict but respected the jury's decision.
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who was widely criticised for her handling of the fires, said in a statement that "no verdict can bring back the lives lost or erase the pain families have endured".
"So many are still struggling to rebuild," she said. "For those still displaced, the devastation remains a daily reality."
Prosecutors had argued that Rinderknecht was driven by revenge, anger and loneliness because he had nowhere to go for the holiday.
They cited geolocation data from his iPhone, security camera footage that showed his car's location and witness testimony from passengers.
They alleged that Rinderknecht had a "deeply entrenched belief that the wealthy were destroying the world" and in turn purposely started the blaze in the affluent neighbourhood.
The fire was one of several that ignited back-to-back across the LA region in January, which in total left 31 people dead and destroyed 16,000 structures.

title: An effort to circumvent the Electoral College may be within reach. But hurdles remain
summary: A national effort to ensure that only winners of the popular vote become president could reach a critical milestone soon.
text:
An effort to circumvent the Electoral College may be within reach. But hurdles remain
A national effort to ensure that only winners of the popular vote become president could reach a critical milestone soon.
It's a possible outcome of huge Democratic wins in this month's midterm elections.
Next year, Democrats will fully control five states that could sign the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement among states to award their presidential electoral votes to the winner of the nationwide popular vote, not the winner of their respective states.
If they do join other 18 Democratic-led states — plus the District of Columbia — that are in the compact, the effort will have surpassed the needed 270 electoral votes required to go into effect, making an end run around the Electoral College. So far no Republican-led states have joined the compact and the party is largely not unified on the issue.
There are still plenty of political, practical and legal hurdles that this effort would need to clear. But proponents are optimistic many of those hurdles will be cleared – even perhaps in time for the next presidential election.
"I've never been more confident that 63% of American voters can get what they want in the 2028 presidential election, which is a national popular vote for president." Patrick Rosenstiel, a senior consultant to National Popular Vote, the group pushing for the compact in states across the country, told NPR, referencing Pew polling.
Right now, the compact has a total of 222 electoral votes. The five states that will soon be completely in the hands of Democrats – Arizona, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Nevada and Wisconsin – add up to 61 electoral votes. Combinations of at least four of those states would put the compact over 270.
So far, governors and incoming governors in Pennsylvania and Nevada have said they are open to signing legislation that would bring their states into the interstate agreement. But other governors have yet to publicly weigh in.
One of the looming questions over these efforts is whether these states – all presidential battlegrounds – would be willing to give up their immense influence in elections ahead of the 2028 presidential contests.
And leaders in each state will also have to weigh whether they want to be the tipping point in moving forward a movement that could upend how the U.S. decides presidential winners.
Already, some Democrats are more reticent on the issue than they were before. For example, Democratic Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs, who had previously supported the measure, has not commented recently on whether the state's new Democratic majorities should sign on. NPR reached out to Hobbs' office for comment but did not receive a response before publication.
And then of course, there are the various legal and logistical hurdles.

US declassifies more UFO footage filmed in the Middle East
The US government released an eighth tranche of records regarding Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAPs), marking the latest step in an effort to declassify government files on UFOs.

title: They were fined $811m for conning detained migrants, but the scams didn't stop
summary: How convicted fraudsters made millions from detained immigrants, evaded efforts to shut down their bail business and left migrants behind bars.
text:
They were fined $811m for conning detained migrants, but the scams didn't stop
- Published
Every morning for a month, Mildred Juarez woke up at five to be the first person in the showers at the immigration centre in Texas where she was being detained. Her friends had paid her bail, and she wanted to look presentable when she was finally released.
But every day, she was told her bond had not been paid.
Juarez was confused. Her friends had wired $2,600 (£1,970) to a bond company, Libre Immigration Services (LIS), that had been recommended by her lawyer. LIS said it would begin "the process of paying her immigration bond". But the next day came, and the day after that, with no release.
What she didn't know was that LIS was owned by a convicted fraudster, who had acquired the assets of another bail company co-founded by two men who also had fraud convictions. These two men were fined $811m in 2024 for scamming their clients.
Their firm, Libre By Nexus, which was at one point the largest immigration bail company in America, had appeared to shut down after federal regulators caught up with them.
But public records and BBC interviews with clients and former employees reveal a tangle of interconnected operations continued - along with the flow of cash - while leaving immigrants stuck in detention centres.
Since President Donald Trump has returned to office after promising an immigration crackdown, Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has made over 1.2m arrests, and fast-tracked deportations. The administration has tried unsuccessfully to make it illegal to give migrants bail but the sharp increase in detentions has increased demand for bond companies to secure bail and their release.
Conditions in these centres can be poor. Held in custody, away from family, often scared to speak out, many have faced health problems and endured inadequate food or treatment, according to immigrant advocates and reports by the US government.
In the detention centre where Juarez was locked up, she and about 100 other detainees slept in bunks laid out in rows in a cacophonous room. The lights were left on all night and guards routinely woke everyone up for roll call. According to Castro and advocacy groups, detainees who caused trouble were put in "the hold" - solitary confinement.
The White House and officials from Homeland Security did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.
For Juarez, the wait to be bailed out of detention seemed interminable.
In an email to the BBC, a spokesperson for LIS said Juarez "misunderstands" their services - that they are not bondsmen themselves, but they connect detained individuals to those who are licensed bondsmen. They said another company ultimately decided not to work with her.
An email sent by LIS, and reviewed by the BBC, said that the company had paid a cash bond to ICE on behalf of Juarez. The message was forwarded to Juarez as proof of payment a few days before her release.

title: Anthropic says it will put humanity first. Will its IPO change that?
summary: Critics say now that the AI giant is a public company, its commitment to put safety ahead of commercial success will be tested.
text:
Anthropic says it will put humanity first. Will its IPO change that?
As Anthropic executives and co-founders gathered to celebrate the artificial intelligence company's market debut at the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday, CEO Dario Amodei spoke about AI's potential benefits, and risks, to humanity.
"There is a gigantic difference between how AI will go if we pay little attention to safety versus how it will go if we are obsessed with safety," Amodei said before ringing the ceremonial opening bell. "And an obsession with safety and public benefit has been built into Anthropic's DNA from the start."
Anthropic raised a record $81.3 billion from the IPO and a further $26 billion through a separate private placement, surpassing SpaceX and vaulting into the ranks of publicly traded companies worth more than $1 trillion.
The company has built its reputation on the promise that developing safe AI matters more than winning the race for commercial dominance. It has cultivated an image as an AI safety pioneer, presenting itself as a company willing to put humanity's long-term interests ahead of industry competition.
But now that Anthropic is a public company, that commitment faces a new test. The IPO has brought in new investors, greater scrutiny and pressure to deliver returns to shareholders. Some critics question whether the company can stay true to its founding mission.
The commercial demands of being a public company may cloud safety decisions that could negatively impact the company's share price, such as delaying the release of potentially risky models, legal experts told NPR.
Anthropic's concerns about AI safety are not merely part of its public messaging. Amodei has repeatedly warned about the potential threats advanced AI models pose to humanity, particularly if they escape the control of their developers. The company's IPO prospectus echoed those concerns, warning that "sufficiently advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly."
Anthropic also acknowledged that it may ultimately lose control of its own models.
"There can be no assurance, however, that the safeguards or access regimes we adopt will prove adequate, that we will correctly identify which capabilities require restriction, or that constraints we impose will not be circumvented," the company warned investors.
Anthropic's founders and employees just got very rich
Anthropic's corporate structure is intended to protect its mission, even as it pursues commercial success. Anthropic is a public benefit corporation (PBC), meaning its board must balance shareholder interests with its social mission.
As part of that structure, the company has installed an oversight body known as the Long-Term Benefit Trust, which has the power to appoint four of the company's seven directors. The founders effectively control the appointment of the remaining three.

title: Birds killed in blaze at one of the largest foie gras farms in the US
summary: Hundreds of young birds were also rescued from the fire, which comes as foie gras is under renewed scrutiny over animal welfare concerns.
text:
Birds killed in blaze at one of the largest foie gras farms in the US
- Published
A fire broke out at one of the largest foie gras farms in the US on Thursday, killing an undetermined number of birds.
The blaze engulfed several barns at Hudson Valley Farms in upstate New York before firefighters could get inside. No information has been provided as to what caused the fire.
Crews managed to rescue hundreds of young birds and hatchlings, and no workers or first responders were injured, according to local news outlets.
Foie gras, made from the fattened liver of a duck or goose, has long drawn protests from animal rights groups because the birds are force-fed. Voters in both Washington DC and Denver backed bans on foie gras sales in this month's midterm elections.
Marcus Henley, manager of Hudson Valley Foie Gras in Ferndale, New York, told local news outlet Radio Catskill that the fire destroyed two buildings housing ducks and geese.
"The building isn't there anymore," Henley said, adding that he suspected an electrical malfunction may have started the blaze, although this has not been confirmed.
The company does not disclose how many birds it hosts at one time. Commercial poultry farms can typically house thousands of birds.
Westchester News 12 reported that the emergency response to the fire in the early hours of Thursday morning involved 37 fire departments and 200 first responders.
The fire spread rapidly, and the metal-clad, wood-frame structure of the building made it difficult for firefighters to stop the flames from spreading inside the barn.
Hudson Valley Foie Gras and the local fire department did not respond to a request for comment.
Foie gras producers have long been criticised by animal rights groups due to the production process, which involves the force feeding of birds through plastic tubes, which allows them to gain over a third of their body weight in a short period of time.
New York moved to ban the product in 2019, and Hudson Valley farms have been in litigation with the state since.
At a city council hearing in 2019, Henley argued against the ban, saying that journalists who visited the farm found "nothing inhumane" about their practices.
Animal rights activist group PETA told the BBC that they will erect a billboard nearby in memory of the birds who perished, and encouraged Hudson Valley farms to donate surviving birds to local sanctuaries.
